{{< new-terms >}}

## PCA turns many columns into one map

A table with many columns cannot be drawn in one picture. **Principal component analysis**
(PCA) builds new axes from the old columns, so that the first two hold as much of the
spread as any two axes can. Plotted on those two, the rows form a map on which similar rows
sit close together. Ecologists call such a map of samples an **ordination**, and PCA is the
most widely used way to make one.

The community matrix has 24 taxon columns. Pairs of them make `r choose(24, 2)` scatter
plots, and none shows the whole community. This page builds the map for it, shows how to
read its axes from their **loadings**, and checks the axes against the recorded depth and
seabed.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Each component is the direction of most remaining spread

PCA finds the direction through the data along which the points spread out most. That
direction is the first **principal component**, PC1. The second, PC2, is the direction of
most remaining spread at right angles to the first, and so on: there are as many
components as columns, ordered by how much of the variance each holds. Keeping the first
two or three keeps as much of the spread as two or three numbers can.

::: {.diagram}
![PCA finds the direction of most spread through the data (PC1) and the next at right angles to it (PC2), then reads each point's position along the new axes. Loadings are the weights that build a component from the columns; a score is a point's value on a component; components are ordered by the share of the variance they hold.](img/principal-components.svg){fig-alt="Two cards joined by an arrow, with a strip of definitions below. 1 Find the directions: a cloud of grey points on column A against column B stretches diagonally up to the right; an orange arrow labelled PC1 runs along the longest spread and a shorter blue arrow labelled PC2 at right angles to it. One point is drawn in black. 2 Read the points on them: the same cloud turned so that PC1 runs left to right and PC2 upwards; a dashed line drops from the black point to the PC1 axis, labelled its score on PC1. The strip below reads: loadings, the weights that build a component from the columns, for example PC1 = 0.8 × A + 0.6 × B; score, a point's value on a component, where it sits along that new axis; variance, components are ordered by the share of the spread they hold, PC1 the most."}
:::

Each component is a weighted sum of the original columns. The weights are its
loadings, one per column, and they say what the component is made of. A station's
value on a component is its **score**: its position along that axis of the map.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The maths, if you want it
With the columns of $X$ centred and scaled, take the eigen-decomposition of their
correlation matrix $S = X^\top X / (n-1)$:

$$S v_j = \lambda_j v_j , \qquad \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_p$$

The eigenvector $v_j$ holds the loadings of component $j$, the score of station $i$ is
$x_i^\top v_j$, and the eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ is the variance of that component. The share
of the variance it holds is $\lambda_j / \sum_k \lambda_k$.
:::

## The columns are scaled first, and a component's sign is arbitrary

The columns are put on a common scale first, for the reason
[Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) gave: otherwise the column with the largest
numbers takes over the first component. And a component's sign is arbitrary. Flipping
every loading and every score gives the same axis pointing the other way, so "high on PC1"
means nothing until the loadings say which end is which.

## Worked example

### The first two components hold under a third of the variance

The community matrix gets the log and common scale of
[Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd), and then `step_pca()`, which adds the
components to the recipe. `num_comp = 2` keeps the first two as columns for the map; the
recipe still records the variance of all 24, and `tidy()` reads it back. scikit-learn's
`PCA` does the same job at the end of a pipeline.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fit-pca
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()
community <- load_coastal_community()
taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax"))

pca_recipe <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |>
  step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(all_numeric_predictors(), num_comp = 2)

pca_prep <- prep(pca_recipe)

# Step 3 of the recipe is the PCA.
variance <- tidy(pca_prep, number = 3, type = "variance") |>
  filter(terms %in% c("percent variance", "cumulative percent variance")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = terms, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::select(-id)

variance |> slice_head(n = 6) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 1)))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()
community = load_coastal_community()
taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax")

pca_pipeline = Pipeline([
    ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")),
    ("normalise", StandardScaler()),
    ("pca", PCA()),
]).fit(taxa_only)
pca = pca_pipeline["pca"]

variance = pd.DataFrame({
    "component": np.arange(1, pca.n_components_ + 1),
    "percent variance": 100 * pca.explained_variance_ratio_,
})
variance["cumulative percent variance"] = variance["percent variance"].cumsum()

variance.head(6).round(1)
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: variance-numbers
#| include: false
pct <- variance$`percent variance`
pct2 <- variance$`cumulative percent variance`[2]
```

PC1 holds `r round(pct[1], 1)`% of the variance and PC2 `r round(pct[2], 1)`%, so the map
shows `r round(pct2, 1)`% of it. From PC3 on, each component holds between
`r round(pct[3], 1)`% and `r round(pct[24], 1)`%.

A share that low is usual for counts of species. Two stations of the same kind rarely give
the same counts: chance alone makes counts vary, and that variation is spread across all
24 columns, so no one direction can hold much of it. The share of the variance tells you
how much of the total spread the map shows, not whether what it shows is real.
[How many components to keep](dimensionality-reduction.qmd) asks which components carry
structure; this page reads the first two.

### Loadings place each taxon by depth and seabed

`tidy(type = "coef")` returns the loadings; in scikit-learn they are the rows of
`components_`. The table shows the five taxa with the largest loadings on PC1, either sign.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: loadings
loadings <- tidy(pca_prep, number = 3, type = "coef") |>
  filter(component %in% c("PC1", "PC2")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = component, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::select(taxon = terms, PC1, PC2)

loadings |>
  slice_max(abs(PC1), n = 5) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

## Python

```{python}
loadings = pd.DataFrame(pca.components_[:2].T, columns=["PC1", "PC2"])
loadings.insert(0, "taxon", taxa_only.columns)

(loadings.loc[loadings["PC1"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index]
    .head(5)
    .round(3)
    .reset_index(drop=True))
```

:::

The two tabs give the same loadings with opposite signs, on both components. Both are
correct: R and scikit-learn settle the arbitrary sign by different conventions.
The rest of this page reads R's signs; on scikit-learn's, the map is turned upside down
and left to right.

A table of 48 loadings is hard to read. The figure puts each taxon at its loadings on
PC1 and PC2, and adds two things the PCA never saw, worked out from the survey: the
average depth at which the taxon was counted (weighted by its counts), and the share of
its counts made on hard bottom.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: taxon-habitat
stations_habitat <- community |>
  inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id")

taxon_habitat <- stations_habitat |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("tax"), names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
  summarise(mean_depth = weighted.mean(depth_m, count),
            hard_share = weighted.mean(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), count),
            .by = taxon) |>
  inner_join(loadings, by = "taxon")
```

```{r}
#| label: loading-numbers
#| include: false
n_hard_taxa <- sum(taxon_habitat$hard_share > 0.5)
centre <- taxon_habitat |> filter(sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2) < 0.05)
n_centre <- nrow(centre)
hard_station_share <- mean(stations_habitat$substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"))
deep_corner <- taxon_habitat |> filter(hard_share < 0.5) |> slice_min(PC1, n = 1)
shallow_corner <- taxon_habitat |> filter(hard_share < 0.5) |> slice_min(PC2, n = 1)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-loadings
#| fig-cap: "Each taxon placed by its loadings on the first two components. Colour is the share of its counts made on hard bottom; the label is the average depth at which it was counted, in metres. Neither was given to the PCA."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'glue::glue("Scatter plot of loading on PC2 against loading on PC1, one point per taxon, labelled with its average depth in metres and coloured by the share of its counts on hard bottom. The taxa lie around a ring. The {n_hard_taxa} taxa counted mostly on hard bottom, in yellow, sit together in the upper right. The taxa counted mostly on soft bottom run round the lower and left side, from shallow at the lower right to deep at the upper left. {n_centre} taxa sit at the centre, labelled close to the survey average depth of {round(mean(stations_habitat$depth_m))} m.")'
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.6
ggplot(taxon_habitat, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = hard_share)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = round(mean_depth)), size = 3.1, seed = 1,
                  show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_percent(),
                         name = "counts on\nhard bottom") +
  labs(x = "loading on PC1", y = "loading on PC2")
```

:::

The taxa lie around a ring, and where each one sits matches its habitat.

- The `r n_hard_taxa` taxa counted mostly on hard bottom sit together in the upper right.
  No other taxon is there.
- The rest run round the lower and left side in order of depth, from
  `r round(shallow_corner$mean_depth)` m at the bottom to
  `r round(deep_corner$mean_depth)` m at the far left.
- `r n_centre` taxa sit at the centre, with loadings near zero on both components. Their
  average depths, `r round(min(centre$mean_depth))` to `r round(max(centre$mean_depth))` m,
  are close to the survey's `r round(mean(stations_habitat$depth_m))` m, and
  `r round(100 * min(centre$hard_share))`–`r round(100 * max(centre$hard_share))`% of their
  counts were on hard bottom, close to the `r round(100 * hard_station_share)`% of stations
  there. They follow neither depth nor seabed, and PCA gave them almost no weight without
  being told.

So both components mix depth and seabed. A taxon's angle round the ring says which mix of
the two it follows, and its distance from the centre says how strongly.

### Depth and seabed run diagonally across the components

The scores place the stations on the map. Correlating them with the recorded depth and
seabed shows which way each increases across it. Correlation runs from −1 to 1, and taken
together the two correlations give a direction on the map: an arrow along PC1 for a
variable that correlates with PC1 alone, diagonal for one that correlates with both.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: directions
stations <- community |>
  bind_cols(bake(pca_prep, new_data = NULL)) |>
  inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate),
             by = "station_id") |>
  mutate(hard_bottom = substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"))

directions <- tibble(
  variable = c("depth", "hard bottom"),
  PC1 = c(cor(stations$PC1, stations$depth_m), cor(stations$PC1, stations$hard_bottom)),
  PC2 = c(cor(stations$PC2, stations$depth_m), cor(stations$PC2, stations$hard_bottom))) |>
  mutate(angle_from_PC1 = atan2(PC2, PC1) * 180 / pi)

directions |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 2)),
                     angle_from_PC1 = round(angle_from_PC1))
```

## Python

```{python}
scores = pca_pipeline.transform(taxa_only)
stations = community.assign(PC1=scores[:, 0], PC2=scores[:, 1]).merge(
    survey[["station_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id")
stations["hard_bottom"] = stations["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"])

directions = pd.DataFrame({
    "variable": ["depth", "hard bottom"],
    "PC1": [stations["PC1"].corr(stations["depth_m"]),
            stations["PC1"].corr(stations["hard_bottom"].astype(float))],
    "PC2": [stations["PC2"].corr(stations["depth_m"]),
            stations["PC2"].corr(stations["hard_bottom"].astype(float))],
})
directions["angle_from_PC1"] = np.degrees(np.arctan2(directions["PC2"],
                                                     directions["PC1"]))
directions.round(2).round({"angle_from_PC1": 0})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: direction-numbers
#| include: false
dir <- directions |> mutate(off_axis = abs(angle_from_PC1) %% 90,
                            off_axis = pmin(off_axis, 90 - off_axis))
depth_dir <- filter(dir, variable == "depth")
hard_dir <- filter(dir, variable == "hard bottom")
r2 <- \(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
between <- abs(depth_dir$angle_from_PC1 - hard_dir$angle_from_PC1)
```

Depth correlates `r r2(depth_dir$PC1)` with PC1 and `r r2(depth_dir$PC2)` with
PC2; hard bottom correlates `r r2(hard_dir$PC1)` and `r r2(hard_dir$PC2)`.
Neither belongs to one axis. Depth increases along a direction
`r round(depth_dir$off_axis)`° from the nearest axis, and hard bottom along one
`r round(hard_dir$off_axis)`° from it, where 45° would be exactly halfway between two
axes. The two directions are `r round(between)`° apart, close to a right angle.

The variance table explains it. PC1 and PC2 hold almost the same share,
`r round(pct[1], 1)`% and `r round(pct[2], 1)`%. When two directions carry nearly equal
spread, every direction in the plane they make carries nearly the same spread too, so
which one PCA takes as PC1 is close to arbitrary. PCA has found the plane in which depth
and seabed vary, and on the map both are clear. It has no way to know which two
directions in that plane matter to an ecologist. Naming PC1 "the depth axis" because depth
correlates with it would be wrong here: a component is a direction of large variance, and
nothing makes it line up with one driver.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-ordination
#| fig-cap: "The 800 stations on the first two components, coloured by depth and shaped by seabed. The arrows point the way depth and hard bottom increase, from their correlations with the two components; neither runs along an axis."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'glue::glue("Scatter plot of PC2 against PC1 for {nrow(stations)} stations. Colour runs from dark purple for shallow stations to yellow for deep ones, a smooth ramp with no edge in it. Hard-bottom stations, drawn as circles, form an arm towards the upper right; soft-bottom stations, drawn as triangles, form an arm running from the bottom up to the left. Two arrows leave the origin: depth points up and to the left, hard bottom up and to the right, each about {round(mean(dir$off_axis))} degrees from the nearest axis.")'
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.6
arrows <- directions |> mutate(x = 5 * PC1 / sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2),
                               y = 5 * PC2 / sqrt(PC1^2 + PC2^2))

ggplot(stations, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = depth_m,
                 shape = if_else(hard_bottom, "Hard bottom", "Soft bottom")),
             size = 1.9, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 0.7,
               colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) +
  geom_label(data = arrows, aes(x = 1.18 * x, y = 1.18 * y, label = variable),
             colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4, label.size = 0) +
  labs(colour = "depth (m)", shape = NULL)
```

:::

The map shows the two kinds of structure that the earlier pages met. Hard-bottom stations
form an arm of their own that meets the soft-bottom arm only in a narrow band: that is the
boundary [Clustering with k-means](clustering.qmd) found. Depth shading runs smoothly
along each arm with no edge anywhere: a gradient, which k-means and the tree could only cut
at an arbitrary depth. A grouping cannot show that difference; the map shows both at once.

## PCA sees straight-line directions

PCA finds directions of variance, and only straight ones. A taxon that peaks at middle
depths is captured only roughly, and along a long gradient the stations bend into an arch
on the map, which ecologists call the **horseshoe effect**. A single station with extreme
counts can also pull a component towards itself, so look for isolated points before
reading the axes.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- **Principal component analysis** builds new axes from the columns, ordered by the
  variance they hold, each at right angles to the last. The first two make a map of the
  stations, an **ordination**.
- **Loadings** are the weights that build a component; a station's position on it is its
  **score**. Read a component from its loadings, and only after checking its sign: R and
  scikit-learn gave opposite signs here.
- The first two components held `r round(pct2, 1)`% of the variance. For counts of
  species that is usual, and it does not mean the map shows nothing.
- A component is not a gradient. Depth and hard bottom both ran about
  `r round(mean(dir$off_axis))`° from the nearest axis, because PC1 and PC2 held nearly
  equal variance. PCA finds the plane, not the drivers within it.
- On the map, the seabed shows as a boundary between two arms and depth as a smooth
  gradient.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Remove `step_normalize()` from the recipe, keeping the log. Which taxa now have the
   largest loadings on PC1, and what do they have in common?
2. Colour the station map by `season` from the survey instead of by depth. Does season
   line up with either component?
